A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Fast SceneScript by the same authors, with matching core methods and experiments. All supplied text, equations, tables and figures support comparison. v1 ends with references; v2 includes supplementary Sections A-D.

before.justification: Tables 1-3 report original layout-estimation experiments on ASE and Structured3D, including models trained by this work and component ablations.

after.justification: v2 retains the original experiments and adds SceneCAD evaluation, object-detection results, and original supplementary sensitivity analyses and training controls.

M1.justification: Section 3.3 changes the reported projection sub-block architecture from two ReLU activations to one, consistent with v2 Figure S7. This is a limited architecture-description revision; the PDFs do not establish whether implementation changed or the description was corrected. MTP, SSD, CGD, their losses and head sharing otherwise remain unchanged.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates layout estimation on synthetic ASE and Structured3D. v2 adds real-world SceneCAD and evaluates 3D object detection on both ASE and SceneCAD. ASE detection covers cabinet, chair, table, sofa and bed, substantially broadening both task and domain coverage.

E2.justification: The existing SceneScript, SceneScript+MTP, RoomFormer, ProductThre and SoftmaxThre comparisons are retained. Table S4 adds the ground-truth-supervised confidence variant CGD, GT as a comparator. Extending existing baselines to detection and SceneCAD does not itself change their membership; TR3D supplies annotations rather than serving as an evaluated baseline.

E3.justification: Existing layout protocols are retained. New detection experiments introduce an ASE 19k/1k train/test split, generated bounding-box annotations, and F1 evaluation at 0.25 and 0.50 IoU. Appendix B specifies detection training budgets and SceneCAD fine-tuning. Additional experiments vary head counts and thresholds and compare 60- versus 90-epoch SceneScript training.

E4.justification: The original ablations remain as Table 4. Tables S1-S5 add 12/16-head tests, scoring-threshold sweeps, confidence-supervision tolerance tests, ground-truth versus first-head supervision, and a longer-training baseline control. New analyses examine classwise and detection token-score distributions and show failures on incomplete point clouds and non-Manhattan scenes. The Structured3D visualization is relocated, not newly added.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental seed counts, repeated-run variability, confidence intervals or significance tests. The new confidence-score distributions and discussion of model uncertainty concern token predictions, not uncertainty estimation for experimental performance.

E6.justification: Original Tables 1-2 and v1 Table 3, now Table 4, retain their numbers. New results include SceneCAD layout SSD at 0.556 F1 and 42 ms versus SceneScript at 0.556 and 108 ms, and ASE detection SSD at 0.829 F1@0.50 and 104 ms versus 0.823 and 535 ms. Supplementary tables add sensitivity and control outcomes. Table S2 inconsistently reports 16.10 M parameters for ProductThre/SoftmaxThre versus 15.05 M in retained Table 4.

T1.justification: Equations (1)-(5), the numerical-token consistency criterion and the training objectives remain unchanged. Appendix B.1 and Figure S6 explain the existing confidence-label construction with explicit head indices. No new theorem, proof or substantive mathematical derivation is introduced.

C1.justification: The title, abstract, contributions and conclusion broaden the work from efficient 3D layout estimation to 3D scene understanding encompassing layout and object detection on synthetic and real-world data. The introduction adds a 5.14-fold detection-speedup claim alongside the retained 5.09-fold layout claim. The central MTP, filtering and parameter-efficiency contributions remain.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations involving MTP regularization, inter-head agreement as a confidence-learning signal, and layout-token redundancy versus detection-token structure. It also discusses limited SceneCAD training data and explicitly identifies incomplete point clouds and non-Manhattan layouts as failure conditions. These substantially extend v1's discussion of softmax reliability and decoding tradeoffs.

D1.justification: v2 discloses the default CGD threshold of 0.90, teacher-forcing confidence-label construction, residual projection-block diagrams, detection annotation generation, task-specific training schedules and ASE split-file names. Existing optimizer, learning-rate, batch-size and layout-training details move to Appendix B largely unchanged. The split-file references do not themselves supply their contents.

R1.justification: v2 adds references for MMDetection3D, TR3D and AdamW to support annotation generation and training details. The existing literature and first-use-of-MTP positioning are retained. The layout-estimation related-work subsection moves from Section 2.2 to Appendix C without a substantive change in its research positioning.

P1.justification: The title and selected introductory and concluding passages are revised around scene understanding. Experiments are separated into layout and detection sections, while layout-related work and training details move to the supplement. Most existing method and results prose remains closely matched, so the editorial reworking is limited despite substantial new scientific content.

P2.justification: v2 substantially expands the visual presentation with new benchmark and ablation tables, distribution plots, failure examples, and training and architecture diagrams. v1 Figure 6 moves to Figure S1, and Figures 7-8 become Figures 6-7. Existing displays also undergo placement, caption and styling adjustments; these relocations are distinct from the new visual content.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially addresses v1's limited evidence for applicability beyond synthetic layout estimation through real-world SceneCAD and object-detection experiments. Sensitivity tests, confidence-supervision comparisons, a longer-training control, failure cases and implementation details make the method better supported and more assessable. Limitations remain: ASE detection uses generated annotations, Table S2 conflicts with Table 4 on parameter counts, and Section 4.4 combines a CGD speedup with an SSD accuracy gain for SceneCAD. These reporting problems qualify some claims but do not outweigh the substantial validation and transparency gains.
